01.note: A young priest had been attacked and killed in the Temple during the priests' race up to the altar. His father came and found the boy still convulsing. He said: May my son's death be an atonement for you; but my son is still alive. The account concludes that the ritual purity of the Temple utensils mattered more to the people than the shedding of blood.
01.why: The Gemara is retelling the killing of this priest and now asks what that closing comment means: had murder become trivial to them, or had purity been exaggerated? From a verse about Manasseh spilling innocent blood, it concludes that bloodshed had become trivial.

people.name: The boy's father
people.about: Father of the young priest who was attacked; he speaks over his dying son.

terms.meaning: Something that wipes away guilt or sin before God. The father bitterly offers his son's death as an atonement for the people.
Temple vessels had to be kept free of ritual impurity, which contact with a corpse would cause. The concern here is for the vessels rather than for the boy's life.
A collection of early teachings from the time of the Mishna, often expanding on it.

01.flag: The STORY segment begins mid-incident: the attack itself is only alluded to in the BEFORE segments, and the father's words end with 'etc.'

02.note: On the festival of Sukkot a priest poured water on the altar. Once a priest, described in the translation as a Sadducee who rejected this rite, poured the water onto his own feet instead. All the people pelted him with their etrogim. From then on they would say to whoever poured the water: Raise your hand, so everyone could see it go onto the altar.
02.why: The Gemara has claimed that the water was poured only with the morning offering. Rav Ashi brings this incident as support: people pelted the priest with etrogim, which they carry in the morning, so the pouring must have happened then.

people.name: Rav Ashi
people.about: The Sage who cites this incident from a mishna as proof.

terms.meaning: A rite performed on Sukkot in the Temple: water was poured on the altar alongside the usual wine.
A citrus fruit that people hold, with a palm branch, during the Sukkot prayers; plural etrogim.
A member of a Jewish group of Temple times that rejected many of the Sages' traditions, including this water rite.

03.note: The mother of the High Priest Rabbi Elazar ben Harsum made him a tunic worth twenty thousand dinars. His fellow priests did not let him wear it, because in it he looked naked. The Gemara objects that priestly garments were woven from six-fold thread, so how could anyone see through it? Abaye answers that it was like wine in a glass cup: the fine linen let his skin show through.
03.why: The Gemara has ruled that a priest may serve in a tunic his own mother made, once he gives it to the public. After the case of Rabbi Yishmael ben Pabi, who did just that, this is a contrasting case where the fellow priests refused the gift.

people.name: Rabbi Elazar ben Harsum
people.about: A High Priest whose mother made him a very costly tunic.

people.name: Abaye
people.about: A Sage who explains how the tunic could be see-through.

terms.meaning: The long linen robe worn by priests in the Temple service.
A coin; twenty thousand dinars marks the tunic as extravagantly expensive.

04.note: Every day Hillel the Elder earned half a dinar. He gave half to the guard of the study hall and lived on the other half with his family. One day he earned nothing, and the guard would not let him in. He climbed onto the roof and sat at the skylight to hear Shemaya and Avtalyon teach. It was a winter Friday and snow fell on him all night. At dawn the teachers noticed the hall was dark, saw a man's shape in the skylight, and found him under three cubits of snow. They pulled him out, washed him, rubbed him with oil and sat him by the fire, saying: This man is worthy of desecrating Shabbat for him.
04.why: The Sages teach that in the heavenly court a poor man who says he was too busy earning a living to study Torah is asked: Were you poorer than Hillel? This story is the proof that poverty is no excuse.

people.name: Hillel the Elder
people.about: A poor laborer who pays to enter the study hall and risks his life to hear Torah.

people.name: Shemaya
people.about: One of the two teachers in the study hall; he notices the hall is dark.

people.name: Avtalyon
people.about: Shemaya's colleague, whom Shemaya calls his brother.

terms.meaning: Friday, the day before the Sabbath; their rescue efforts at dawn fall on Shabbat itself.
A winter month in the Jewish calendar.
Do work normally forbidden on the Sabbath, such as lighting a fire. Saving a life permits this; the teachers say Hillel especially deserves it.
An ancient measure, roughly the length of a forearm, about half a meter.

05.note: Rabbi Elazar ben Harsum had inherited a thousand villages and a thousand ships, yet he spent his days walking from town to town to study Torah. Once his own servants came upon him, did not recognize him, and seized him for forced labor. He begged them: Please, let me go and study Torah. They answered: By the life of Rabbi Elazar ben Harsum, we will not let you go. He had never gone to see his own property; he sat and studied Torah day and night.
05.why: The Sages teach that in the heavenly court a rich man who says he was too busy with his property to study Torah is asked: Were you richer than Rabbi Elazar ben Harsum? This story shows how little his wealth distracted him.

people.name: Rabbi Elazar ben Harsum
people.about: A man of enormous inherited wealth who devoted himself to Torah study instead of his estates.

terms.meaning: Forced labor: being seized to work for a lord or official without pay.

06.note: Nicanor went to Alexandria in Egypt to bring back copper doors for a Temple gate. On the voyage home a storm threatened to drown him. The passengers threw one of the heavy doors into the sea, but the storm went on. When they went to throw the second, Nicanor wrapped his arms around it and said: Throw me in with it. At once the sea calmed. He grieved for the lost door all the way, but when they reached the port of Akko it was poking out from under the side of the ship. Some say a sea creature swallowed it and spat it out onto land.
06.why: The mishna names Nicanor among those remembered well for what they did in the Temple, saying miracles happened to his doors. This teaching spells out the miracles; the Gemara then explains that this is why his gates alone were never replaced with gold.

people.name: Nicanor
people.about: The man who brought copper doors from Alexandria for the Temple and would not give up the second one.

terms.meaning: A great city in Egypt, known for its craftsmen.
A port city on the coast of the Land of Israel.

07.note: The House of Garmu, a family of craftsmen, knew how to make the shewbread for the Temple and refused to teach anyone. The Sages brought bakers from Alexandria instead, who could bake the bread but could not take it out of the oven as well, and their bread grew moldy. Saying that everything God created was for His glory, the Sages sent for the House of Garmu. They would not come until their wages were doubled. Asked why they had kept the secret, they said their family knew the Temple would be destroyed and feared an unworthy man would use the skill for idol worship. They were praised for this: their children never ate fine bread, so no one could say they lived off the shewbread's secret.
07.why: The mishna lists the House of Garmu among those remembered badly for refusing to teach their craft. This teaching tells the full story, which ends by giving them a good reason and praising them.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda
people.about: A Sage who gives a different figure for the family's wages: twenty-four maneh, raised to forty-eight.

terms.meaning: Twelve loaves set out each week on a table in the Temple, made in a difficult shape and meant to stay fresh all week.
A large sum of money, equal to one hundred dinars.
A teaching of the early Sages that was not included in the Mishna.

08.note: The House of Avtinas knew how to prepare the Temple incense and refused to teach anyone. The Sages brought craftsmen from Alexandria who could blend the spices, but their smoke spread every which way instead of rising straight like a stick. Saying that God made everything for His sake, the Sages sent for the House of Avtinas, who came only when their wages were doubled. Asked why they kept the secret, they said their family knew the Temple would be destroyed and feared an unworthy man would use it for idol worship. They were praised: no bride from their homes ever wore perfume, and brides marrying in agreed not to, so no one could say they perfumed themselves with the incense.
08.why: The mishna lists the House of Avtinas among those remembered badly for refusing to teach. Like the House of Garmu just before, the full story ends with a reason that wins them praise.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda
people.about: A Sage who gives a different figure for the family's wages: twenty-four maneh, raised to forty-eight.

terms.meaning: A blend of spices burned in the Temple every day; its smoke was meant to rise in a straight column.
A large sum of money, equal to one hundred dinars.

09.note: Rabbi Yishmael tells that once, while walking on the road, he met a descendant of the House of Avtinas, the family that had kept the Temple incense recipe secret. He said to him: Your fathers tried to increase their own honor and lessen God's. Now God's honor stays as it was, and He has lessened theirs.
09.why: The Gemara has just told how the House of Avtinas guarded their secret. This is the first of several meetings with the family after the Temple fell; the series ends with Rabbi Akiva ruling that they must no longer be spoken of badly.

people.name: Rabbi Yishmael
people.about: A Sage who meets a descendant of the House of Avtinas and rebukes him.

terms.meaning: The family of craftsmen who prepared the incense for the Temple and would not teach the method to others.

10.note: Rabbi Akiva reports what Rabbi Yishmael ben Loga told him. Rabbi Yishmael ben Loga went out to a field to gather herbs with a descendant of the House of Avtinas, and saw the man laugh and cry. He cried, he said, remembering his ancestors' honor, and laughed because God will one day restore it. What reminded him? The smoke-raising herb was right in front of him. Rabbi Yishmael ben Loga asked him to point it out. The man said: We are under an oath not to show it to anyone.
10.why: This is one of a series of meetings with the House of Avtinas after the Temple's destruction. Here the family still guards its secret; in the next, they finally hand it over.

people.name: Rabbi Akiva
people.about: The Sage who passes on this account.

people.name: Rabbi Yishmael ben Loga
people.about: The Sage who went gathering herbs with a member of the House of Avtinas.

terms.meaning: The family of craftsmen who prepared the incense for the Temple and would not teach the method to others.
The secret ingredient that made the Temple incense smoke rise in a straight column.

11.note: Rabbi Yohanan ben Nuri tells that he once met an old man holding a scroll. Asked where he was from, the man said: the House of Avtinas. Asked what he held, he said: a scroll of spices. When Rabbi Yohanan ben Nuri asked to see it, the old man said that while his family flourished they never gave it to anyone, but now here it was, and he should take care with it. When Rabbi Yohanan ben Nuri told this to Rabbi Akiva, Rabbi Akiva said: From now on it is forbidden to speak badly of them.
11.why: This closes the series of meetings with the House of Avtinas after the Temple fell. Ben Azzai then draws a lesson from the craftsmen being called back to their posts: no one can take what God has set aside for another.

people.name: Rabbi Yohanan ben Nuri
people.about: The Sage who meets the old man and is given the scroll.

people.name: Rabbi Akiva
people.about: The Sage who rules, on hearing the story, that the family may no longer be spoken of badly.

terms.meaning: The family of craftsmen who prepared the incense for the Temple and would not teach the method to others.
A written record of the spices and how to blend the Temple incense.

12.note: Doeg ben Yosef's father died and left him a small child with his mother. Every day she measured his height in handbreadths and gave the Temple his weight in gold. Later, when the enemy prevailed over the city, she slaughtered him and ate him.
12.why: Rabbi Elazar reads the verse 'the name of the wicked shall rot' to mean that no one names children after the wicked. Ravina objects with this boy, named Doeg after a wicked biblical figure; the Gemara answers: see what befell him, so the name was a bad omen.

people.name: Doeg ben Yosef
people.about: A boy left fatherless as a small child; his mother doted on him.

people.name: Rabbi Elazar
people.about: A Sage who explains that the names of the wicked are not given to others.

people.name: Ravina
people.about: A Sage who objects to Rabbi Elazar with this incident.

terms.meaning: An ancient measure, the width of a hand, a few inches.

13.note: In the year Shimon HaTzaddik died, he told his companions he would die that year. Asked how he knew, he said: every Yom Kippur an old man dressed and wrapped in white met me, went in with me and came out with me. Today an old man dressed and wrapped in black met me, went in with me, and did not come out with me. After the festival of Sukkot he was ill for seven days and died.
13.why: The Gemara has been listing blessings that were present in the Temple and then faded. This account of the High Priest's death is followed by the signs that changed after him: the priests stopped using God's name in their blessing, and the lots stopped falling as before.

people.name: Shimon HaTzaddik
people.about: A High Priest who foresees his own death from a vision on Yom Kippur.

terms.meaning: The Day of Atonement, the one day a year the High Priest entered the innermost chamber of the Temple, the Holy of Holies.
The autumn festival of booths, which comes a few days after Yom Kippur.

14.note: In the years before the Temple was destroyed, the doors of its Sanctuary would open by themselves. Rabban Yohanan ben Zakkai rebuked them. He said: Sanctuary, Sanctuary, why do you frighten yourself? I know you will be destroyed in the end, and the prophet Zechariah son of Ido has already said of you: Open your doors, O Lebanon, that the fire may devour your cedars.
14.why: This is the last of a list of bad signs in the Temple during the forty years before its destruction. The verse Rabban Yohanan quotes leads the Gemara on to ask why the Temple is called Lebanon.

people.name: Rabban Yohanan ben Zakkai
people.about: A Sage who scolds the Sanctuary doors for opening by themselves.

terms.meaning: The main building of the Temple, which held the inner chamber called the Holy of Holies.
Here a name for the Temple, which was built from the cedars of Lebanon.

15.note: Rabbi Yishmael ben Kimhit, the High Priest, was once talking with an Arab in the market, according to the translation on Yom Kippur, when a drop of the man's spit landed on his clothes. This made him ritually impure, so his brother Yeshevav went in and served as High Priest in his place. So their mother saw two of her sons serve as High Priest on one day.
15.why: The Gemara mentioned Rabbi Yishmael ben Kimhit's huge hands while explaining how the High Priest carries the coal pan and the incense, and now gathers more stories about him.

people.name: Rabbi Yishmael ben Kimhit
people.about: A High Priest made ritually impure by a stranger's spit.

people.name: Yeshevav
people.about: His brother, who served as High Priest in his place that day.

terms.meaning: A state that bars a person from Temple service until it is removed. The Sages treated a non-Jew's spit as causing it.
A man with an unusual bodily discharge, whose spit and touch cause ritual impurity.
The chief priest, who alone performed the Yom Kippur service in the Temple.

16.note: Another time, Rabbi Yishmael ben Kimhit, the High Priest, went out and talked with an officer in the market, and a drop of the officer's spit landed on his clothes. His brother Yosef went in and served as High Priest in his place. Again their mother saw two of her sons serve as High Priest on one day.
16.why: The Gemara is collecting stories about Rabbi Yishmael ben Kimhit. This second incident echoes the first, and leads to the teaching that all seven of his mother's sons served as High Priest.

people.name: Rabbi Yishmael ben Kimhit
people.about: A High Priest, again made unfit to serve by a stranger's spit.

people.name: Yosef
people.about: His brother, who served as High Priest in his place.

terms.meaning: An officer or governor.
The chief priest of the Temple. A High Priest made ritually impure could not serve, and another took his place.

17.note: Kimhit had seven sons, and all of them served as High Priest. The Sages asked her what she had done to deserve this. She said: In all my days, the beams of my house never saw the braids of my hair. They answered: Many women did the same, and it did not help them.
17.why: The Gemara has just told how two of Kimhit's sons each stood in for their brother as High Priest on a single day. This teaching rounds out those stories before the discussion returns to how the High Priest takes a handful of incense.

people.name: Kimhit
people.about: Mother of seven sons who all served as High Priest; the Sages ask her the reason.

terms.meaning: The chief priest of the Temple, who led its most important services.

18.note: When Rabbi Yohanan left Rabbi Elazar, his student, Rabbi Elazar would bow and stand in place until his teacher was out of sight. When Rabbi Elazar was the one leaving, he would walk backward until Rabbi Yohanan could no longer see him. Rava, taking leave of his teacher Rav Yosef, would walk backward until he bruised his legs and the threshold of Rav Yosef's house was covered in blood. People told Rav Yosef, who the translation notes was blind, what Rava was doing. Rav Yosef said to him: May it be God's will that you rise to the head of the whole city.
18.why: The mishna says the High Priest leaves the Holy of Holies walking backward. The Gemara extends this to priests, Levites and Israelites leaving the Temple, and to a student leaving his teacher; these are examples of that last rule.

people.name: Rabbi Elazar
people.about: A student who would not turn his back on his teacher.

people.name: Rabbi Yohanan
people.about: Rabbi Elazar's teacher.

people.name: Rava
people.about: A student who walked backward from his teacher until he bled.

people.name: Rav Yosef
people.about: Rava's teacher, who blesses him when told what he does.

19.note: Rabbi Hanina ben Dosa was walking on the road when rain began to fall on him. He said: Master of the Universe, the whole world is comfortable and Hanina is suffering. The rain stopped. When he got home he said: Master of the Universe, the whole world is suffering and Hanina is comfortable. The rain came back.
19.why: The High Priest prayed on Yom Kippur that the prayers of travelers asking for rain to stop should not be heard. Rav Yosef uses this story to ask what good that prayer did against Rabbi Hanina ben Dosa, whose words God carried out.

people.name: Rabbi Hanina ben Dosa
people.about: A Sage whose prayers stop and restart the rain.

people.name: Rav Yosef
people.about: A Sage who compares Rabbi Hanina's prayer with the High Priest's.

terms.meaning: A way of addressing God in prayer.

20.note: A High Priest once made his prayer long. His fellow priests decided to go in after him, and as they began to go in, he came out. They asked why he had prayed so long. He said: Does it trouble you that I prayed for you and for the Temple not to be destroyed? They told him not to make a habit of it, as they had learned that the High Priest did not draw out his prayer, so as not to frighten the people.
20.why: The mishna says the High Priest kept his prayer short; this incident, taught by the Sages, shows the reason given for that rule.

terms.meaning: The chief priest, who on Yom Kippur entered the innermost room of the Temple alone and said a prayer there.
A collection of early teachings from the time of the Mishna, often expanding on it.
